column1: Honey never goes off
column2: Honey is so low in water and so acidic that bacteria cannot grow in it. Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that were still edible.
column3: The right chemistry beats any preservative.

column1: Your body has more bacterial cells than you might think
column2: Current estimates put the bacteria in and on a human body at roughly the same number as human cells, about 38 trillion. Most live in the gut.
column3: You are an ecosystem, not a single organism.

column1: Water can boil and freeze at the same time
column2: At its triple point, about 0.01°C and very low pressure, water exists as solid, liquid and gas at once. Scientists use it to calibrate thermometers.
column3: Everyday substances behave strangely at the edges.

column1: Bananas are slightly radioactive
column2: Bananas contain potassium, and a small fraction of natural potassium is radioactive potassium-40. You would need to eat millions at once for it to matter.
column3: Dose, not presence, decides danger.

column1: Glass is not a slow-moving liquid
column2: Old church windows are often thicker at the bottom, but that comes from how medieval glass was made and fitted. At room temperature glass would take far longer than the age of the universe to flow visibly.
column3: A tidy explanation is not always the true one.

column1: Lightning is hotter than the Sun's surface
column2: A lightning bolt can heat the air around it to about 30,000°C. The surface of the Sun is roughly 5,500°C.
column3: Brief events can be astonishingly extreme.

column1: Humans share about 60 percent of genes with bananas
column2: Many basic cell functions use genes common to almost all living things. Roughly 60 percent of human genes have a recognisable counterpart in bananas.
column3: All life runs on a shared toolkit.

column1: Sound travels faster in water than in air
column2: Sound moves at about 343 metres per second in air and around 1,480 in water. Whales can hear each other across hundreds of kilometres.
column3: The medium shapes the message.

column1: Hot water can sometimes freeze faster than cold
column2: This is called the Mpemba effect, after a Tanzanian student who noticed it in 1963. Scientists still argue over when and why it happens.
column3: Simple questions can stay open for decades.

column1: Your stomach gets a new lining every few days
column2: Stomach acid is strong enough to damage tissue, so the cells lining your stomach are replaced every few days. Mucus adds another protective layer.
column3: Constant renewal is a survival strategy.

column1: Diamonds and pencil lead are the same element
column2: Both are pure carbon. In diamond the atoms form a rigid 3D lattice; in graphite they form flat sheets that slide over each other.
column3: Structure can matter more than ingredients.

column1: Octopuses have three hearts
column2: Two hearts pump blood through the gills and one pumps it around the body. Their blood is blue because it uses copper-based haemocyanin to carry oxygen.
column3: Evolution finds more than one way to solve a problem.

column1: A teaspoon of neutron star would weigh billions of tonnes
column2: Neutron stars pack more mass than the Sun into a ball about 20 kilometres across. A teaspoon of that material would weigh around a billion tonnes or more.
column3: Matter can be crushed beyond imagination.

column1: Your brain uses about a fifth of your energy
column2: The brain is around 2 percent of body weight but uses roughly 20 percent of the energy you burn at rest. Thinking is expensive.
column3: Intelligence comes at a metabolic cost.

column1: Penicillin was found by accident
column2: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed mould killing bacteria on a dish left out over a holiday. Turning it into a usable medicine took more than a decade of work by others.
column3: Discovery needs luck and long follow-through.

column1: Some metals melt in your hand
column2: Gallium melts at about 29.8°C, below body temperature. A spoon made of it would melt in hot tea.
column3: Solid depends on the temperature you live at.

column1: Hiccups may be a leftover from our ancestors
column2: One theory links hiccups to breathing reflexes in amphibian ancestors that gulped air and water. The jury is still out.
column3: Our bodies carry echoes of deep evolutionary history.

column1: The human eye can detect a single photon
column2: Experiments suggest people can sometimes sense a single photon in total darkness. Most of the time, though, the brain filters out such weak signals.
column3: Our senses are sharper than our attention.

column1: Mercury thermometers were phased out for safety
column2: Mercury is toxic, and broken thermometers could release vapour. Many countries have restricted mercury thermometers, replacing them with digital or alcohol ones.
column3: Safety often wins over tradition, slowly.

column1: Air is mostly nitrogen, not oxygen
column2: The air you breathe is about 78 percent nitrogen and only about 21 percent oxygen. The rest is mostly argon, with a tiny share of carbon dioxide.
column3: The obvious ingredient is often not the main one.

column1: Fingerprints form before birth
column2: Ridges on your fingertips form by around the 17th week of pregnancy. Even identical twins have different fingerprints.
column3: Small random differences make us unique.

column1: Antibiotics do not work on viruses
column2: Antibiotics target structures found in bacteria, such as cell walls. Viruses lack these, so colds and flu are not helped by antibiotics.
column3: The right tool depends on the right diagnosis.

column1: Rainbows are actually full circles
column2: From the ground, the horizon cuts off the lower half of a rainbow. From a plane you can sometimes see the full circle.
column3: Our viewpoint hides much of the picture.

column1: Your bones are constantly being rebuilt
column2: Cells in your skeleton break down old bone and lay down new bone all the time. Over about a decade, much of your skeleton is replaced.
column3: Even the solid parts of us are always changing.

column1: Atoms are mostly empty space
column2: If an atom's nucleus were the size of a marble, the atom would be about the size of a football stadium. Almost all the mass sits in that tiny centre.
column3: Solid things are mostly nothing at all.

column1: Your nose can tell apart a huge number of smells
column2: A 2014 study suggested humans could distinguish over a trillion odours, though other scientists challenged the maths. Either way, it is far more than once thought.
column3: Our senses are underrated.

column1: A single bolt of lightning carries huge energy
column2: A typical lightning flash carries about a billion joules. But it lasts so briefly that capturing it is impractical.
column3: Power and usefulness are different things.

column1: Earth's core is about as hot as the Sun's surface
column2: Scientists estimate the inner core is around 5,200°C. It stays solid because of enormous pressure.
column3: Pressure can change how matter behaves.

column1: Sweat itself has almost no smell
column2: Body odour comes mostly from bacteria breaking down sweat on the skin. Fresh sweat is nearly odourless.
column3: The smell is the side effect, not the cause.

column1: Light can bend around gravity
column2: Massive objects like galaxies bend light passing nearby. Astronomers use this gravitational lensing to see even more distant objects.
column3: Gravity can act like a lens.

column1: Your ears keep growing
column2: Ears and noses appear to get larger with age, partly because cartilage and skin change over time.
column3: Bodies keep changing all life long.

column1: Plants can be grown without soil
column2: Hydroponics grows plants in water with dissolved nutrients. Many supermarket herbs and lettuces are grown this way.
column3: Soil is helpful, not essential.

column1: Sunsets are red because of scattering
column2: When the Sun is low, its light passes through more air. Blue light scatters away, leaving reds and oranges.
column3: The same physics makes the sky blue by day.

column1: Some frogs can freeze solid and survive
column2: The wood frog can have much of its body water freeze in winter. Glucose acts as antifreeze in its cells, and it thaws in spring.
column3: Life finds a way through extremes.

column1: Your heart beats around 100,000 times a day
column2: At about 70 beats per minute, that is roughly 2.5 billion beats in an average lifetime.
column3: Steady repetition adds up.

column1: Water expands when it freezes
column2: Most substances shrink as they solidify, but ice is less dense than water. That is why ice floats and pipes can burst.
column3: Exceptions to rules can shape whole planets.

column1: Stars twinkle because of Earth's air
column2: Moving layers of air bend starlight slightly. Planets twinkle less because they appear as tiny discs rather than points.
column3: What you see depends on what is in between.

column1: Sharks existed before trees
column2: Sharks appear in the fossil record over 400 million years ago. The first true trees evolved around 385 million years ago.
column3: Some designs are just very good.

column1: Humans glow faintly
column2: The body gives off a tiny amount of visible light from chemical reactions. It is about 1,000 times too weak for our eyes to see.
column3: There is more around us than we perceive.

column1: DNA in one cell is about two metres long
column2: Stretched out, the DNA in a single human cell would be roughly two metres long. It is packed tightly into a nucleus too small to see.
column3: Packing is a superpower.

column1: Venus flytraps count
column2: A Venus flytrap closes only when trigger hairs are touched twice within about 20 seconds. That avoids wasting energy on raindrops.
column3: Simple counting saves energy.

column1: Some bacteria can eat plastic
column2: In 2016 scientists in Japan found a bacterium that breaks down PET plastic. Researchers are studying its enzymes to speed up recycling.
column3: Nature adapts to what we leave behind.

column1: You are taller in the morning
column2: Discs in your spine compress during the day. You can be about a centimetre shorter by evening.
column3: Gravity works on you all day.

column1: Most dust in homes is not dead skin
column2: Studies suggest much household dust comes from outdoors, tracked in on shoes or blown in. Skin is part of it, but not most.
column3: Common facts deserve a second look.

column1: Helium is running low on Earth
column2: Helium is light enough to escape into space once released. Most is collected from natural gas fields, and supplies are limited.
column3: Even the most common element in stars can be scarce here.

column1: Electric eels can produce 600 volts
column2: They use special cells called electrocytes, stacked like batteries. The shock stuns prey and deters predators.
column3: Biology invented batteries first.

column1: Your brain cannot feel pain
column2: The brain has no pain receptors, so surgeons can operate while patients are awake. Headaches come from surrounding tissues.
column3: The organ that feels everything feels nothing itself.

column1: Earth is not a perfect sphere
column2: It bulges at the equator because of its spin. The diameter at the equator is about 43 kilometres larger than pole to pole.
column3: Spin shapes planets.

column1: Pure water does not conduct electricity well
column2: Dissolved salts and minerals make water conductive. Very pure water is a poor conductor.
column3: It is the impurities that carry the current.

column1: The placebo effect can be real
column2: Patients given inactive treatments sometimes report genuine improvements, especially in pain. Expectations can change how the body responds.
column3: Belief has measurable effects.

column1: The speed of light is a cosmic speed limit
column2: Nothing with mass can reach light speed. At about 300,000 kilometres per second, light could circle Earth over seven times in a second.
column3: Some limits are built into physics.

column1: Kidney stones can come from too little water
column2: Not drinking enough lets minerals concentrate in urine and form crystals. Staying hydrated is a key prevention.
column3: Simple habits prevent painful problems.

column1: Gold is mostly from colliding stars
column2: Many heavy elements, including gold, are thought to form when neutron stars collide. The gold in jewellery may be older than the Earth.
column3: You may be wearing stardust.

column1: Your skin is your largest organ
column2: For an adult, skin covers around two square metres. It protects, regulates temperature and senses the world.
column3: The outside of you is an organ too.

column1: Ants can lift many times their body weight
column2: Some ants can carry objects many times heavier than themselves. Their small size makes this easier than it would be for large animals.
column3: Strength scales strangely with size.

column1: Carbon dating has a limit
column2: Radiocarbon dating works on organic material up to about 50,000 years old. After that, too little carbon-14 remains to measure.
column3: Every tool has a range.

column1: Your gut has its own nervous system
column2: The enteric nervous system has hundreds of millions of neurons. It can run digestion with little input from the brain.
column3: There is a second brain in your belly, of sorts.

column1: Snowflakes are not all unique, technically
column2: Simple tiny snow crystals can look identical. Large, complex snowflakes are almost certainly all different.
column3: The truth often depends on the detail.

column1: Mosquitoes find you partly by your breath
column2: They detect carbon dioxide from many metres away, then use heat and smell to close in.
column3: Breathing gives you away.

column1: Cooking may have helped make our brains bigger
column2: Some scientists argue cooking made food easier to digest, freeing energy for brain growth. It remains a debated theory.
column3: Technology may have shaped our biology.

column1: Saliva starts digestion
column2: An enzyme in saliva, amylase, begins breaking down starch in your mouth. Chew bread long enough and it starts to taste sweet.
column3: Digestion starts before you swallow.

column1: Blue whales have hearts the size of a small car
column2: A blue whale's heart can weigh around 180 kilograms. Its heartbeat can be detected from kilometres away.
column3: Size changes everything.

column1: Rust is slow burning
column2: Rusting and burning are both reactions with oxygen. Rust happens slowly; fire happens fast and releases heat and light.
column3: Same chemistry, different speed.

column1: Your eyes see upside down
column2: The lens of your eye projects an upside-down image onto the retina. Your brain flips it the right way up.
column3: Perception is partly construction.

column1: Bones are stronger than steel by weight
column2: Gram for gram, bone can be stronger than some steels. It is light, flexible and constantly repaired.
column3: Living materials can rival engineered ones.

column1: Tears differ by cause
column2: Scientists distinguish basal, reflex and emotional tears. Their chemical make-up varies.
column3: Even tears have types.

column1: Some trees are thousands of years old
column2: A Great Basin bristlecone pine in California is over 4,800 years old. It was already old when the pyramids were built.
column3: Slow and steady can last millennia.

column1: A day on Earth is getting longer
column2: Tidal friction from the Moon is slowing Earth's spin. Days lengthen by about 1.8 milliseconds per century.
column3: Even time is changing.

column1: The appendix may have a purpose
column2: It was long thought useless, but some research suggests it stores helpful gut bacteria. The question is still being studied.
column3: Calling something useless can be premature.

column1: Microwaves heat water molecules
column2: Microwave ovens make water molecules vibrate, producing heat. Food with more water heats faster.
column3: Invisible waves do everyday work.

column1: Yawning may cool the brain
column2: One theory says yawning brings in cooler air to regulate brain temperature. Why yawns are contagious is still debated.
column3: Common behaviours can still be mysteries.

column1: The Dead Sea lets you float
column2: Its water is about ten times saltier than the ocean. The high density pushes swimmers up.
column3: Density decides what sinks.

column1: Sound can break glass
column2: If a sound matches a glass's natural resonant frequency and is loud enough, the vibrations can shatter it.
column3: The right frequency beats raw force.

column1: Cows produce methane mostly by burping
column2: Microbes in a cow's stomach produce methane as they digest grass. Most is released through burps, not the other end.
column3: Details matter in climate science.

column1: Diamonds can burn
column2: Heat a diamond to around 700–900°C with oxygen and it will burn, turning into carbon dioxide.
column3: Forever is relative.

column1: Your fingernails grow faster than toenails
column2: Fingernails grow around 3 millimetres a month. Toenails grow more slowly, roughly a third as fast.
column3: Different parts age at different speeds.

column1: Lobster blood is colourless until exposed to air
column2: It contains copper-based haemocyanin, which turns blue when it binds with oxygen.
column3: Colour can be a chemical signal.

column1: Light from distant stars may be very old
column2: Some stars we see are thousands of light years away. Their light left them thousands of years ago.
column3: Looking up is looking back.

column1: Ice can be one of many types
column2: Scientists have identified around 20 different forms of solid water. Most only exist at extreme pressures.
column3: Even familiar substances have hidden variety.

column1: Fireflies make cold light
column2: Fireflies produce light through a chemical reaction that wastes almost no energy as heat.
column3: Nature built efficient lighting long ago.

column1: Tomatoes are botanically fruit
column2: Botanically, a fruit develops from a flower and contains seeds. Tomatoes, cucumbers and peppers all qualify.
column3: Kitchen and science categories differ.

column1: Laughing is contagious for a reason
column2: Hearing laughter activates brain regions that prepare us to laugh too. It may help bond groups together.
column3: Shared emotion is social glue.

column1: Your sense of smell is linked to memory
column2: Smell signals travel close to brain areas for memory and emotion. That is why a scent can bring back a vivid moment.
column3: Memory has a nose.
